title: Teacher Cognition — What Teachers Believe

pts: Teacher cognition research examines teachers' knowledge, beliefs, and thinking, and how these shape actual classroom decisions.
Much of this cognition is tacit — teachers often can't fully articulate the beliefs driving their moment-to-moment choices.
This field extends Unit 72's brief introduction into a full, established area of educational research.
points.who: Simon Borg's research on language teacher cognition

v: Teachers or trainee teachers in pairs
A 10-minute video or audio recording of one’s own lesson

items: Record ten minutes of a lesson, with the head teacher’s permission and without filming learners’ faces.
Watch it with a colleague. Pause at three or four decision points: a correction, a change of plan, a question.
At each pause, explain what you were thinking and why. The colleague asks only open questions.
Note any belief you expressed that you had not put into words before.
Without recording, a colleague observes and notes decision points; discuss them the same day.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A stimulated recall conversation (written for this book):

lines: B: Here you stopped the group work early. What were you thinking?
A: The noise. I thought the head teacher would come.
B: Was the noise a problem for learning?
A: No, they were on task. I stopped because I believe a quiet class is a good class. I did not know I still believed that.

blocks.x: Stimulated recall is a common research method in teacher cognition, and it can also be used for professional development (Borg 2006). The teacher’s explanation is an interpretation made after the event, not a perfect record of the moment, but it can surface tacit beliefs.

body: Purpose: to show stimulated recall. Content: two teachers at a laptop showing a paused classroom video, one pointing at the screen, with a thought bubble revealing a belief. Style: warm, realistic. Board version: a rectangle screen with a pause symbol and a thought bubble.

items: A phone camera or voice recorder; VLC media player (free, open source) for pausing and replaying.

blocks.x: A colleague’s written notes of decision points, discussed the same day.

pts: Teachers' actual classroom practice sometimes diverges from their stated, consciously articulated beliefs about teaching.
This gap isn't hypocrisy — it reflects how much classroom decision-making happens below conscious, deliberate reflection.
This connects to Unit 25's philosophy-articulation exercise — making beliefs explicit is itself valuable precisely because of this common gap.

v: A belief questionnaire; an observation checklist

items: Complete a short belief questionnaire on four topics: error correction, home-language use, group work and grammar teaching.
Over two weeks, ask a colleague to observe two lessons with a checklist on the same four topics, or keep a tally yourself.
Compare the two records topic by topic.
Where they differ, write one possible reason in your journal. Unit 25’s philosophy statement is a useful companion.
Teachers in a cluster do this in pairs and share only the patterns, not individual results.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Belief: Learners should speak English most of the time. Observation: teacher talk 80% of lesson time; learners spoke English in two short answers each.
Belief: Home languages are a resource. Observation: teacher said ‘English only, please’ three times.

blocks.x: The gap between stated and enacted belief is widely reported and is not hypocrisy (Phipps and Borg 2009). Stated beliefs are often ideals; practice is shaped by habit, time, examinations and classroom management. The gap is useful because it shows where change is possible.

body: Purpose: to show the stated–enacted gap. Content: two overlapping outlines of the same teacher, one labelled ‘what I say I believe’, one ‘what I do’, with partial overlap. Style: simple. Board version: two overlapping circles.

items: Google Forms (free) for the belief questionnaire, with results kept private.

blocks.x: A paper questionnaire and a tally sheet.

pts: Teachers' foundational beliefs about teaching often form during their own years as students, long before formal teacher training begins.
This 'apprenticeship of observation' can be remarkably resistant to change, even after extensive contradictory training.
Recognising this origin helps explain why some training-recommended practices are adopted only superficially.
points.who: Dan Lortie's Apprenticeship of Observation concept

items: Participants recall an English teacher they had in school and describe one typical lesson in detail.
They list three things that teacher believed about teaching, judging by what they did.
In pairs, compare these beliefs with their own.
Discuss which beliefs came from training and which from their own schooling.
Participants write the memory in their home language first, then discuss in English.
Support: prompts such as How did the teacher correct mistakes? Who spoke most?
Challenge: identify one inherited belief to test through action research (Unit 67).

blocks.x: A trainee’s memory (written for this book):

lines: Our teacher in Class 8, in a Kannada-medium school in Mandya, read each lesson aloud, explained it in Kannada, and dictated answers. We copied them and learned them by heart. I scored well.
Beliefs inferred: The teacher’s explanation is the main source of learning. Correct answers come from the teacher. Memorizing is learning.
T: Which of these do you still believe?
S1: The last one, a little. It worked for me.

blocks.x: Lortie (1975) called this the apprenticeship of observation: pupils watch teachers for many years, but see only the visible performance, not the reasoning behind it. Such beliefs can persist through training.

body: Purpose: to show where beliefs originate. Content: a timeline from a child at a school bench to an adult teacher at the board, with small thought bubbles collecting along the way. Style: warm, Indian school setting. Board version: a line with a small figure at each end.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited number of boards) for anonymous sharing of memories in a large course.

body: Lortie’s (1975) Schoolteacher was a sociological study of American teachers, but its concept of the apprenticeship of observation has been used in teacher education research across many countries, including research on language teachers (Borg 2003).

pts: Beliefs act as a filter, shaping which training content a teacher genuinely internalises versus merely performs when observed.
This explains why identical professional development can produce very different practical outcomes across different teachers.
Effective professional development increasingly targets belief examination directly, not just technique transmission.

v: A training module recently delivered; follow-up observation notes

items: Choose one practice promoted in a recent in-service training, for example pair work or formative assessment.
Recall or collect follow-up observations from four or five teachers who attended.
Classify how each teacher used it: adopted fully, adapted, used on the surface, not used.
For each case, discuss which beliefs might explain the response. Plan one change to the next training that addresses beliefs directly.
Before the next training, run a short belief survey and use the results to plan discussion time.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Observation notes from a follow-up (written for this book):

lines: Teacher 1: Pairs talk about the text. Adopted.
Teacher 2: Pairs read the same answer aloud together. Surface use: pairs, but no interaction.
Teacher 3: Not used. ‘The class becomes noisy and the syllabus is long.’
A: Teacher 2 did what we asked, in form.
B: But if she believes learning means reciting correct answers, pair work will become pair recitation.

blocks.x: Beliefs act as a filter on new ideas (Pajares 1992). Programmes that only transmit techniques may produce surface change; programmes that make beliefs discussable are more likely to change practice.

body: Purpose: to show how beliefs filter training. Content: training ideas pouring into a funnel with a mesh labelled ‘beliefs’; some ideas pass into the classroom, some are reshaped, some are blocked. Style: clear. Board version: a funnel with arrows.

items: Google Sheets (free) for recording follow-up observations across schools.

blocks.x: A paper observation grid shared at a cluster meeting.

pts: Beliefs change most reliably through sustained reflective practice and direct classroom evidence, not through being told a different view.
This connects directly to Unit 67's action-research cycle — evidence from one's own classroom is a particularly powerful belief-change mechanism.
This is why this entire series has favoured reasoning and evidence over simple prescription wherever possible.

items: Choose one belief you hold with some doubt, for example My learners cannot do group work.
Design a small test: try a structured group task (Unit 34) in two lessons.
Collect simple evidence: the number of learners on task, the English produced, a quick learner feedback slip.
Write whether the evidence supports, challenges or complicates the belief.
Two teachers test the same belief in different classes and compare results.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s note (written for this book):

lines: Belief tested: My Class 7 cannot work in groups; it becomes noisy.
Evidence: With roles (reader, writer, timekeeper, reporter), 11 of 12 groups finished the task. Noise was high but on task. 38 of 45 feedback slips said ‘I liked it’.
Conclusion: They can, with roles and a time limit. I need a signal to stop.

blocks.x: Guskey (2002) argued that teachers’ beliefs often change after they see improved outcomes from a new practice, not before. This is why action research (Unit 67) is a powerful route to belief change.

body: Purpose: to show the sequence of practice, evidence and belief change. Content: three steps: ‘try a new practice’, ‘see learner results’, ‘belief shifts’, with a learner group smiling at the second step. Style: clean. Board version: three boxes with arrows.

items: Google Forms (free) for a two-question learner feedback slip.

blocks.x: Paper feedback slips and a tally.

points.sub: How it develops over a career
pts: Novice teachers often hold more rigid, rule-based beliefs; experienced teachers typically develop more flexible, context-sensitive ones.
This mirrors this series' own progression from Tier I's foundational rules toward Tier III's principled, contextual judgement.
This connects to Unit 72's career-stage development — cognition itself matures alongside practical skill.

items: Give a trainee and an experienced teacher the same scenario: Halfway through a lesson, you realize most of the class has not understood the task.
Each writes separately what they would do and why.
Compare the answers. Note differences in how many options each considers and what they notice.
Discuss how the experienced teacher’s reasoning developed. Link to Unit 68 on mentoring.
Use a short video clip of a classroom moment instead of a card.
Support: trainees choose from three options before explaining.
Challenge: trainees predict the mentor’s answer before seeing it.

lines: Trainee: Explain the instructions again, more slowly, then continue.
Experienced teacher: Check who has understood. Ask one group to demonstrate. Cut the task in half so we still reach the report stage. Next time, show an example before starting.

blocks.x: The experienced response notices more, considers more options and connects this moment to future lessons. Research on expertise suggests that novice teachers often rely on rules and plans, while experienced teachers draw on flexible, context-sensitive knowledge built from many cases (Tsui 2003). Experience alone does not guarantee this: expertise requires reflection on experience.

body: Purpose: to show the development of cognition. Content: a path from a novice holding a rulebook to an experienced teacher surrounded by many small case cards. Style: friendly. Board version: two stick figures, one with a book, one with many small cards.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared bank of scenarios and responses.

pts: Institutional pressures can force a gap between a teacher's genuine beliefs and their actual required practice.
This connects to Unit 71's discussion of institutional constraints — cognition operates within, and is constrained by, larger systemic forces.
Understanding this helps distinguish a teacher's genuine pedagogical stance from institutionally-imposed compromise.

items: Each participant lists three things they do in class that they would not do if free to choose.
For each, name the constraint: examination, syllabus pace, class size, school rules, parental expectations.
Groups sort the constraints into ‘within my control’, ‘partly in my control’ and ‘outside my control’.
For one partly controllable constraint, plan a small change. Unit 73 discusses high-stakes testing pressures.
DIET faculty collect anonymous lists from a cluster to inform district planning.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One participant’s list (written for this book):

lines: I dictate model answers. Constraint: board examination format. Control: partial.
I rarely do speaking. Constraint: speaking is not examined; parents ask for marks. Control: partial.
I teach in rows. Constraint: fixed benches. Control: partial (turn-and-talk is possible).
A: So my beliefs are not the problem here. The system is.
B: Partly. But which of these could we change a little?

blocks.x: Borg (2006) shows that contextual factors, such as prescribed curricula and examinations, often explain why teachers do not act on their beliefs. Distinguishing belief from constraint prevents unfair judgements of teachers in observation and appraisal.

body: Purpose: to show cognition within context. Content: a teacher figure inside a frame whose sides are labelled ‘exams’, ‘syllabus’, ‘class size’, ‘expectations’; the teacher’s thought bubble extends beyond the frame. Style: clear. Board version: a stick figure inside a rectangle with four labels.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) for anonymous collection of constraints.

body: When observing a colleague, ask ‘What stopped you from doing it differently?’ before giving advice. The answer often reveals a constraint, not a belief, and advice that ignores the constraint will not be taken up.

pts: Periodically and honestly examining your own beliefs against your actual observed practice reveals genuine, often surprising gaps.
This connects directly to Unit 9's reflective practice and Unit 25's philosophy articulation, now grounded in this research field.
This reflective habit, more than any single belief, is what distinguishes cognitively mature, expert practice.

items: At the start of term, write five beliefs about teaching English, each in one sentence.
For each, write one piece of classroom evidence you could collect to check it.
During the term, collect the evidence through observation, recordings or learner work.
At the end of term, revise each belief as ‘kept’, ‘changed’ or ‘uncertain’, and write the reason. Compare with Unit 9’s reflective cycle and Unit 25’s philosophy statement.
Share the audit with a mentor (Unit 68) once a year.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A sample audit entry (written for this book):

lines: Belief: Correcting every error helps accuracy.
Evidence: Recorded two speaking lessons; counted corrections and whether learners repeated the correct form later.
Result: Learners repeated the correction at once but used the old form again ten minutes later.
Revised belief: Uncertain. Immediate correction may help less than I thought. Try delayed feedback (Unit 8) next term.

blocks.x: The habit of testing beliefs against practice, more than any single belief, marks mature professional cognition (Borg 2006; Richards and Lockhart 1994).

body: Purpose: to show a regular reflective routine. Content: a cycle of ‘state beliefs’, ‘plan evidence’, ‘collect evidence’ and ‘revise beliefs’, with a small notebook at the centre. Style: calm. Board version: a circle with four labels.

items: Google Docs (free) or Microsoft OneNote (free) for a digital journal.

blocks.x: A paper teaching journal with one page for each belief.

body: Write the one belief about teaching that you feel most certain of. Plan one simple way to collect evidence about it from your own class this month. Record what you find, even if it confirms the belief.

dek: Unit 79 of 100: teachers' often-implicit beliefs about language and learning shape classroom practice as powerfully as any formal training — a field worth understanding directly.

aims.x: Two teachers attend the same training, use the same textbook and teach similar classes, yet teach very differently. Much of the difference lies in what they believe about language, learners and teaching, often without ever having put it into words. This unit introduces teacher cognition, the research field that studies these beliefs and their relation to practice. It extends the brief treatment of teacher identity in Unit 72, and its activities are designed for teachers, trainee teachers and teacher educators, including DIET faculty who plan in-service programmes.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: define teacher cognition and explain why much of it is tacit;
explain why stated beliefs and observed practice often differ, without treating the gap as hypocrisy;
describe the apprenticeship of observation and its effect on training;
explain how beliefs filter professional development;
design professional development that works with evidence from teachers’ own classrooms;
compare novice and experienced teacher cognition;
distinguish a teacher’s beliefs from institutional constraints on practice;
use a structured routine to examine your own beliefs against your practice.

why: Why this matters. Two teachers with identical training can teach very differently, because their underlying, often unexamined beliefs about learning differ.

background.x: Research on teaching once focused mainly on observable behaviour: which teacher actions were associated with learner gains. From the 1970s, educational researchers began to study teachers’ thinking and decision-making as well (Clark and Peterson 1986). In language teaching, Simon Borg’s review drew together a growing body of work on what language teachers think, know and believe, and how this relates to what they do (Borg 2003). He showed that cognition is shaped by teachers’ own schooling, their professional education and their classroom experience, and that it interacts with contextual factors in complex ways (Borg 2006).

The field uses several overlapping terms: beliefs, knowledge, attitudes, maxims and personal theories. Pajares (1992) called teacher beliefs a ‘messy construct’, because they are hard to define and hard to observe directly. Researchers therefore combine methods: interviews, stimulated recall (in which teachers watch recordings of their own lessons and explain their decisions), observation and journals. Each method has limits, and a teacher’s account of a decision is not the same as the decision itself.

Teacher cognition has direct implications for teacher education. Lortie (1975) argued that teachers arrive at training having already spent many years observing teachers, which gives them strong, largely unexamined ideas about what teaching is. Training that ignores these ideas may be adopted only on the surface. This helps explain a familiar pattern in large in-service programmes: teachers use the new vocabulary in workshops, but classrooms change less than expected.

In India, this matters on a large scale. NEP 2020 calls for continuous professional development for teachers and for teacher education that develops reflective practitioners (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). DIETs, Block and Cluster Resource Centres and state initiatives reach very large numbers of teachers through cascade training. Research on cognition suggests that such programmes are more likely to change practice if they include opportunities for teachers to surface their beliefs, try new practices and examine evidence from their own classrooms (Guskey 2002).

items: Stimulated recall report. A short account of three decision points in one’s own lesson, with the beliefs they revealed.
Gap analysis. A comparison of a belief questionnaire with observation data, with possible reasons for each difference.
Training redesign. For teacher educators, a revised session plan that includes belief discussion and follow-up evidence.
Belief audit. A term’s record of five beliefs, the evidence collected and the revisions made.
Which belief about teaching do you hold most strongly? Where did it come from?
When did evidence from your own classroom last change your mind?
Which of your practices are driven by constraints rather than beliefs?
How do in-service programmes you know address teachers’ existing beliefs?
How has your thinking about teaching changed since your first year?
What would a colleague learn about your beliefs by watching one lesson?

Guskey, T. R. 2002. ‘Professional development and teacher change’. Teachers and Teaching: Theory and Practice 8/3: 381–91.

perm: Recording lessons requires school permission and, where learners are identifiable, consent from parents or guardians. Delete recordings after use unless consent covers keeping them.

All conversations, memories, observation notes, questionnaires and audit entries are written for this book. Recording lessons for stimulated recall requires school permission and, where learners are identifiable, parental consent; recordings should be deleted after use. Screenshots of Google Forms, Sheets, Docs, Padlet, Mentimeter, VLC or OneNote require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: Lortie’s (1975) term for the many hours future teachers spend watching their own teachers as pupils, which shapes their beliefs about teaching before any training begins.
A reflective cycle in which a teacher states some beliefs about teaching, collects classroom evidence about them, and records any revisions over a term.
The way teachers’ existing beliefs screen new ideas, so that techniques which conflict with those beliefs may be adopted only on the surface (Pajares 1992).
Features of a teaching context, such as large classes, examinations and limited resources, that may prevent teachers from acting on their beliefs.

The continuing learning and growth of teachers throughout their careers, through training, reflection, collaboration, observation and classroom research; it is most effective when sustained and linked to daily practice.

The distinction between what teachers say they believe about teaching and the beliefs visible in their actual classroom practice (Phipps and Borg 2009). The gap is common, reflects constraints such as examinations and time, and is useful for reflection.

A research method in which participants watch a recording of their own actions, such as a lesson, and explain what they were thinking at particular moments (Gass and Mackey 2000). It helps reveal teachers’ tacit decision-making.

Knowledge that people use in practice but find hard to put into words (Polanyi 1966). Much of teachers’ expertise, such as knowing when to move on, is tacit and can be explored through stimulated recall.
What teachers know, believe and think, and how this relates to what they do in the classroom (Borg 2003). It is shaped by schooling, training, experience and context.

The knowledge, skill and judgement that develop as teachers gain experience and reflect on it, allowing them to read situations quickly and respond flexibly. Experience alone does not guarantee expertise; reflection and learning are essential.
